title: Blue Screen / System Crash
cardText: Diagnose Windows blue screen crashes, stop codes and recurring system instability.
Investigate crash dumps, drivers, updates, RAM, storage, system files and hardware faults.
Identify the likely cause before replacing components or reinstalling Windows.
text: This guide covers recurring Windows blue screen and stop-code errors.
Start by recording the stop code and checking the Windows crash history.
Use available crash logs to narrow down drivers, software or hardware problems.
Check recent changes, memory, storage and Windows system files where appropriate.
Back up important data before performing major repairs or recovery operations.

checkBlueScreenCode.title: Record the Windows stop code
body: Record the exact stop code shown when Windows crashes.
Examples include MEMORY_MANAGEMENT, CRITICAL_PROCESS_DIED, PAGE_FAULT_IN_NONPAGED_AREA and IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL.
Record any driver or system file name displayed alongside the code.
Check whether the same stop code appears repeatedly or whether different errors occur.
A stop code is a starting point for diagnosis, not proof that a particular component has failed.
If the computer restarts too quickly to read the code, inspect the Windows crash history or dump files.

checkCrashHistory.title: Check Windows crash history
body: Press Windows + R, enter perfmon /rel and press Enter.
Reliability Monitor shows a timeline of application failures, Windows errors and unexpected shutdowns.
Select a date corresponding to a blue screen and inspect the critical events.
Open View technical details where available to check for bugcheck information.
Record the dates, error codes and any component or application mentioned.
Look for a pattern connecting the first crash to a driver, update or hardware change.

link.name: Microsoft: Reliability Monitor command
link.description: Official documentation for opening Reliability Monitor using perfmon /rel.

checkCrashHistory.alt: Windows Reliability Monitor showing critical system failures on a dated timeline
checkCrashHistory.caption: Reliability Monitor helps identify recurring crashes and when they first occurred.

checkCrashDumps.title: Check Windows crash dump files
body: Open File Explorer and check C:\Windows\Minidump for recent .dmp files.
Also check whether C:\Windows\MEMORY.DMP exists.
These files may contain technical information about the system when it crashed.
If dump files are available, an experienced technician can inspect them using Microsoft WinDbg.
In WinDbg, open the dump file and run !analyze -v for detailed bugcheck analysis.
Record the bugcheck code and any consistently identified third-party driver.
A driver name or module mentioned in a dump is not always the root cause.
Crash dumps can contain sensitive system information, so avoid sharing them publicly.

link.description: Official guidance for examining crash dumps and interpreting bugchecks with WinDbg.

link.name: Microsoft: WinDbg documentation
link.description: Microsoft's Windows debugging tools and crash analysis reference.

investigateCrashEvidence.title: Investigate the crash evidence
body: Compare the bugcheck code, dump analysis and crash history.
Check whether a particular third-party driver repeatedly appears in the failures.
Look for hardware error records, memory-related failures or storage-related stop codes.
If the evidence points to a driver, investigate that driver first.
If no component can be identified confidently, continue with the standard troubleshooting checks.
Avoid replacing hardware based only on a generic stop code.

checkRecentChanges.title: Check recent hardware and software changes
body: Determine whether the blue screens began after installing a driver, Windows update, application or hardware component.
Check recently installed RAM, graphics cards, storage devices and peripherals.
Review changes to BIOS settings, XMP, EXPO, overclocking or undervolting.
Compare the timing of the changes with Reliability Monitor's crash history.
If a particular change closely matches the first crash, test reversing it.

link.name: Microsoft: Troubleshoot stop-code errors
link.description: Official guidance for checking newly installed hardware and software.

undoRecentChange.title: Reverse the suspected change
body: Roll back or remove the driver, application or hardware change associated with the crashes.
If new hardware was fitted, test with the previous hardware configuration where practical.
Restore supported default BIOS, memory or overclocking settings if the crashes followed a configuration change.
Make one change at a time so the result can be evaluated.
Monitor stability after each change.

checkWindowsUpdates.title: Check Windows update history
body: Open Settings, Windows Update, Update history.
Check whether a cumulative update, feature update or driver update was installed immediately before the crashes began.
Compare the installation dates with the recorded crash history.
Review any documented issues affecting the installed update.
Do not uninstall updates simply because they are recent.
If the evidence points to a specific update, investigate the supported rollback procedure.

link.name: Microsoft: Windows recovery options
link.description: Official recovery options for Windows after problematic system changes.

rollbackUpdate.title: Remove the suspected Windows update
body: Confirm which Windows update is associated with the start of the crashes.
Open Windows Update, Update history, Uninstall updates where supported.
Remove only the relevant update if Microsoft provides a supported removal option.
Some updates cannot be uninstalled.
If the system cannot start normally, Windows Recovery Environment may provide an Uninstall Updates option.
Check that the BitLocker recovery key is available before recovery operations that may require it.
Restart and monitor stability after the change.

link.name: Microsoft: Windows recovery options
link.description: Official recovery procedures including uninstalling updates and System Restore.

checkDrivers.title: Check device drivers
body: Open Device Manager and look for devices showing warning symbols or error codes.
Review the drivers implicated by crash dumps or recent changes.
Pay particular attention to graphics, chipset, storage and network drivers when relevant.
Compare installed driver versions with the computer or component manufacturer's supported versions.
If a crash began after a driver update, use Device Manager, Properties, Driver, Roll Back Driver where available.
Otherwise update or reinstall the affected driver from a trusted manufacturer source.
Avoid indiscriminately replacing every driver.

link.name: Microsoft: Update or roll back drivers
link.description: Official Device Manager instructions for updating, reinstalling and rolling back drivers.

repairDriverIssue.title: Repair the affected driver
body: Update, roll back or reinstall the driver associated with the crashes.
Use a driver compatible with the installed Windows version and hardware.
If the problem began after an update, try the previous stable driver when available.
Restart Windows after the change if required.
Monitor whether the same stop code or crash returns.

link.name: Microsoft: Driver repair procedures
link.description: Instructions for reinstalling or rolling back a problem driver.

checkSafeMode.title: Test Windows Safe Mode
body: Access Windows Recovery Environment and select Troubleshoot, Advanced options, Startup Settings, Restart.
Select Safe Mode from the startup options.
Safe Mode starts Windows using a limited selection of drivers and services.
Check whether the computer remains stable while performing basic tasks.
If crashes occur only during normal startup, a third-party driver, service or application may be involved.
Safe Mode cannot reproduce every workload, so stability there does not completely rule out hardware problems.
Restart normally after testing.

link.name: Microsoft: Windows Startup Settings and Safe Mode
link.description: Official instructions for entering and exiting Safe Mode.

softwareConflict.title: Investigate software or driver conflicts
body: Review third-party drivers, startup applications, security software and services.
Consider a clean boot to isolate non-Microsoft services and startup applications.
Disable one suspected component at a time and retest normal Windows startup.
Check the crash history after each change.
If the computer continues crashing, investigate memory and other hardware.

link.name: Microsoft: Windows stop-code troubleshooting
link.description: Official troubleshooting for recurring crashes and software conflicts.

checkMemory.title: Test system memory
body: Press Windows + R, enter mdsched.exe and press Enter.
Save open files and select Restart now and check for problems.
Allow Windows Memory Diagnostic to complete.
Check the diagnostic results when Windows restarts.
If errors are reported, investigate individual RAM modules, memory slots and configuration.
If XMP or EXPO is enabled, temporarily test with supported default memory settings.
Passing a basic memory test does not completely exclude intermittent memory instability.

link.name: Microsoft: Windows stop-error troubleshooting
link.description: Official guidance for memory-related Windows crashes and hardware diagnostics.

checkMemory.alt: Windows Memory Diagnostic dialog showing Restart now and check for problems
checkMemory.caption: Use Windows Memory Diagnostic to test for memory faults that may cause blue screens.

investigateMemoryFault.title: Isolate the memory fault
body: Record any memory diagnostic errors.
For desktops, test one RAM module at a time using the motherboard's recommended slot.
Test modules under supported default settings before concluding that the hardware is defective.
Check whether errors follow a specific memory module or slot.
An unstable XMP or EXPO configuration may cause errors without a defective RAM module.
If the cause remains unclear, further memory and motherboard diagnostics may be necessary.

replaceMemory.title: Memory fault or configuration issue identified
body: Testing has isolated a defective RAM module or unstable memory configuration.
Replace the faulty module if a physical defect is confirmed.
If errors occur only with XMP or EXPO enabled, restore stable supported memory settings.
Check motherboard memory compatibility and recommended slot placement.
Run memory diagnostics again and monitor system stability.
If errors persist with known-working RAM, investigate the motherboard or memory controller.

checkStorageHealth.title: Check SSD or HDD health
body: Review SSD or HDD SMART information using a suitable manufacturer diagnostic utility.
Check Windows System event logs for disk, storage controller or repeated I/O errors.
Check available free space on the Windows system drive.
A failing drive or storage controller can cause crashes and operating system corruption.
If the drive reports critical warnings or media failures, protect the data before running intensive tests.
If no storage fault is evident, continue with Windows system file checks.

link.name: Microsoft: Windows stop-code troubleshooting
link.description: Guidance covering storage issues, free space and hardware-related crashes.

replaceStorage.title: Storage fault identified
body: The storage device has reported errors indicating a possible hardware fault.
Back up important data immediately if accessible.
Confirm the faulty device using manufacturer diagnostics or other reliable evidence.
Replace the drive if a hardware defect is confirmed.
Restore the operating system and user data as appropriate.
Retest Windows stability after repairing the storage problem.

checkSystemFiles.title: Check Windows system file integrity
body: Open Command Prompt or Windows Terminal as administrator.
Run DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth
After DISM completes, run sfc /scannow
DISM checks and repairs the Windows component store used by system file repair.
SFC checks protected Windows system files and repairs corruption where possible.
Allow both commands to finish and record their results.
If corruption is repaired, restart Windows and retest stability.

link.name: Microsoft: Using System File Checker
link.description: Official instructions for running DISM and SFC to repair Windows system files.

repairSystemFiles.title: Retest after Windows system file repair
body: Review the DISM and SFC results to determine whether the repairs completed successfully.
If corruption remains, check Microsoft's guidance for additional repair options.
Restart Windows and test the activities that previously caused crashes.
If the computer remains stable, the system file repair may have resolved the issue.
If blue screens continue, investigate cooling and hardware instability.

link.name: Microsoft: Repair corrupt Windows system files
link.description: Official instructions for further action when DISM or SFC reports corruption.

checkTemperatures.title: Check CPU and GPU temperatures
body: Use a reputable hardware monitoring utility to inspect CPU and GPU temperatures.
Compare readings with the hardware manufacturer's supported temperature limits.
Check for overheating, thermal throttling and abnormal cooling fan behaviour.
Inspect cooling fans, heatsinks, air vents and case airflow.
Do not assume a high temperature is abnormal without checking the component's specification.
Avoid prolonged stress testing if the computer is already overheating or unstable.

resolveCoolingIssue.title: Correct the cooling problem
body: Remove dust from air vents, heatsinks and fans using an appropriate cleaning method.
Check that cooling fans operate normally.
For desktops, verify the CPU cooler is properly mounted and case airflow is unobstructed.
For laptops, check vents and the cooling system according to manufacturer guidance.
After repairs, monitor temperatures and retest the computer.
If temperatures return to normal but crashes continue, inspect Windows event logs.

checkEventViewer.title: Review Windows Event Viewer
body: Press Windows + R, enter eventvwr.msc and press Enter.
Open Windows Logs, System.
Inspect errors around the times of the blue screens.
Look for BugCheck Event ID 1001, recurring WHEA-Logger hardware errors, storage errors and driver failures.
Kernel-Power Event ID 41 indicates an unexpected shutdown but does not identify the underlying fault.
Compare timestamps and error details with the Reliability Monitor history.
Investigate repeated, relevant errors rather than unrelated warnings.

link.name: Microsoft: Advanced Windows stop-error troubleshooting
link.description: Technical reference for collecting and analysing Windows crash information.

link.name: Microsoft: Kernel-Power Event ID 41
link.description: Explains why Event ID 41 alone does not identify the cause of a crash or power loss.

researchCrashCause.title: Investigate recurring crash errors
body: Record the recurring error source, event ID, stop code and any associated driver.
Compare the findings with crash dumps and previous diagnostic results.
Check the official documentation for the implicated driver, device or Windows component.
If WHEA hardware errors are present, investigate the relevant processor, memory, PCIe or hardware subsystem.
Use the evidence to select a targeted repair rather than applying unrelated fixes.

applySpecificFix.title: Apply the targeted repair
body: Apply the repair supported by the identified error and manufacturer documentation.
Make one change at a time.
Restart Windows if required.
Test the workload or conditions that previously triggered the crash.
If crashes continue, check firmware and remaining hardware causes.

checkFirmware.title: Check BIOS and firmware stability
body: Check whether the system uses overclocking, undervolting or memory settings beyond supported defaults.
Review the installed BIOS version and the manufacturer's release notes.
Look for firmware fixes specifically addressing system stability, memory compatibility or hardware errors.
Check storage and graphics firmware only where relevant to the crash evidence.
An older firmware version is not automatically the cause of a blue screen.
Do not attempt a BIOS update when the computer cannot maintain stable power and there is no safe manufacturer-supported recovery method.

updateFirmware.title: Apply the relevant firmware update
body: Confirm that the update is intended for the exact computer or motherboard model.
Read the manufacturer's release notes and instructions before proceeding.
Ensure the computer has a stable power source.
For laptops, meet the manufacturer's charger and battery requirements.
If BitLocker is enabled, confirm the recovery key is available and follow guidance about suspending protection.
Do not interrupt the update.
If reliable power cannot be guaranteed, postpone the update and proceed with further diagnostics.
Retest system stability after the update.

hardwareEscalation.title: Further system diagnostics required
body: Blue screens continue after checking crash evidence, software, drivers, memory, storage, system files and cooling.
Possible causes include motherboard faults, unstable RAM or memory controller, CPU faults, graphics hardware or power delivery problems.
Review any WHEA errors and crash dumps for consistent hardware-related evidence.
For desktops, test with known-working compatible components where practical.
Consider Windows recovery or repair installation only after checking backups and whether a hardware fault remains likely.
Do not replace expensive components based solely on a generic stop code.
Record the stop codes, crash dump findings and completed tests before arranging advanced diagnostics.
